The researchers are clear that this study is not a blueprint for better AI. It only offers a new view of how the brain organizes decisions, with the possibility of someday inspiring AI architecture. As a next step, Vlasov's team plans to dig deeper into the timing of neural signals and develop new techniques for measuring neural activity to see how feedback circuits arise and coordinate across multiple processing layers.
This piece looks inside the protein design institute led by David Baker. The lab, home to about 100 researchers, shares a bundle of deep-learning tools they call an open “collective brain.”
RFdiffusion and the tools that followed it sit at the center. Proteins are now designed from the ground up, with precision down to a single atom.
This kind of AI protein design is rewriting how biotech makes antibodies, enzymes and medicines.

Surface flow in the ocean is a major force driving Earth's climate, but observation alone has long made it hard to see in full. GOFLOW, built by researchers at Tel Aviv University, is an AI system that reconstructs this hidden flow directly from satellite imagery.

GOFLOW learns from satellite images already on hand and draws out the motion of surface ocean currents hidden inside them. The key is pulling dynamical information that was previously hard to access out of existing data, without needing any new observations.

The researchers said this restored flow information sharpens the input data for climate forecasts. Without expanding observations, it opens a path to understanding Earth's climate more deeply using data we already have.
A public AI contest to predict drug metabolism was held. The task was to determine whether a given compound activates the PXR receptor, which clears about half of marketed drugs from the body.
The result: 28 teams tied for first place, statistically speaking. The startup Inductive Bio edged ahead by a narrow margin.
The result shows that in AI drug discovery, what separates performance isn't model size but data quality. It could change how this field evaluates models.

blocks.cap: AI that may not think the way humans do

blocks.x: Computer scientist Peter J. Denning argues that Alan Turing's vision for artificial intelligence may have sent 75 years of AI research down the wrong path.

In his new book 『Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines』, Denning argues that two fundamental assumptions Turing laid down in 1950 still govern AI research today. The first is that intelligence can be reproduced in computer software independent of a physical body; the second is that a machine can demonstrate intelligence simply by imitating a human in conversation, which later became known as the Turing Test.

“These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development,” Denning writes. “My premise is that accepting these claims is what has brought us to the mess we're in with AI today.” He warns that pursuing artificial general intelligence (AGI) is unlikely to succeed, and that the technology could instead introduce major new risks.

At the center of his argument is tacit knowledge — the vast body of human understanding that is hard to put into words or for computers to process. Denning says machine learning fails to capture five branches of tacit knowledge: common sense, everyday interaction with people and environments, emotion and perception, practical performance skills, and the social and historical knowledge embedded in culture.

Attempts to organize common sense into a database go back a long way. Douglas Lenat's Cyc project set out in the 1980s to build a vast collection of common-sense facts, and after 40 years of work has amassed about 25 million entries. Denning notes that “even this trove hasn't provided a common-sense foundation that makes expert systems as smart as real experts,” pointing out that much of the knowledge that makes a person an expert cannot be reduced to propositions.

Practical skill is an even bigger challenge. He points to violinists as an example. “A virtuoso can play beautiful music without being able to explain to a student how they produce it. Even if a robot observes and imitates a skilled person, a robot without a biological body cannot grasp what the performer feels while making beautiful music.” Denning sees all these limits as stemming from a ‘representation problem’: computers can only compute with encoded data, and tacit knowledge does not fit that framework.

“Behind every word is a deep well of tacit knowledge that supports its meaning,” Denning says. “Commonly used large language models like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini only handle words — they don't know or understand the meaning of what they're saying.” He explains that intelligence leans heavily on context, and probing that context leads endlessly back through prior conversation. No matter how large neural networks grow, LLMs cannot acquire the embodied human knowledge we call culture, nor reach the goal of the Turing Test.

Denning concludes that humans and AI may end up with different tacit knowledge that neither can understand in the other. “Machines cannot read our tacit knowledge, and we cannot read theirs. We are strangers separated by an unbridgeable gap.” He argues that if machines cannot read the context behind human intent, aligning advanced AI with human goals could become impossible, and that a greater threat than superintelligent domination is a web of machine intelligence that falls short of human level yet still causes serious problems.

blocks.cap: Artist's impression of the exoplanet K2-18b

blocks.x: K2-18b is one of the most attention-grabbing exoplanets in recent memory. It orbits in the habitable zone of a red dwarf about 124 light-years away in the direction of Leo. James Webb Space Telescope observations revealed an atmosphere rich in carbon dioxide and methane, making it a candidate 'Hycean' planet, where a thick hydrogen atmosphere wraps around an ocean of liquid water.

Because it may hold conditions favorable to life, K2-18b became a major target for the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI). Researchers combed it for artificial radio signals using two of the world's most powerful radio telescopes. According to results published in The Astronomical Journal, the observations captured millions of candidate signals, but turned up no evidence of narrowband radio signals comparable to today's Earth technology.

The project combined data from the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico and MeerKAT in South Africa. Pairing facilities of this scale in a single observing campaign is quite rare, which allowed an unusually sensitive sweep of the K2-18b system.

Just as important as the observations was the processing pipeline that filtered the vast amount of recorded radio signals. Because radio telescopes are constantly flooded with signals originating from Earth, the researchers first sift out interference with sophisticated software. The VLA used the COSMIC (Commensal Open Source Multi Mode Interferometer Cluster) system, and MeerKAT used the BLUSE (Breakthrough Listen User Supplied Equipment) system.

The researchers then used five screening methods to search for traces of technological civilization. First, they applied radio frequency interference (RFI) masking to remove bands already heavily contaminated by human-made transmissions. They also considered the Doppler effect: since radio signals traveling between planets should show Doppler shift, signals with little to no change were treated as originating from Earth and discarded.

Signals with a signal-to-noise ratio below 10 or above 100 were also filtered out. In multi-beam analysis, the telescopes formed multiple focused beams at once, with one aimed at K2-18b and another at a different patch of sky; a genuine signal should appear only in the beam pointed at K2-18b. The final transit filtering method checks whether a signal disappears when the planet passes behind its star, but since this observation had no such 'secondary transit,' it was not used.

Millions of candidate signals turned up, but none passed every stage. Still, the observation allowed the team to set an 'upper limit' on the strength of any radio transmitter that might exist in the K2-18b system, and that limit is roughly comparable to the transmission power of the now-collapsed Arecibo radar facility in Puerto Rico.

Above all, this project showed that automated data-processing pipelines can handle the enormous volume of signals pouring out of modern SETI observations. The value of such techniques will only grow once future observatories like the Square Kilometer Array come online. K2-18b is quiet for now, but the ability to catch traces of technology beyond the solar system keeps improving.

blocks.cap: A phylogenetic tree of scent plants. Green bars mark families rich in sleep-promoting scent molecules.

blocks.x: Food scientists at the National University of Singapore (NUS) used machine learning to screen more than 2,300 scent molecules from aromatic plants, picking out compounds with the potential to aid sleep. The approach could speed up the discovery of natural sleep aids.

Sleep is essential for health, learning and everyday well-being, yet sleep problems affect up to a third of the world's population. Sleep medications help some patients, but they come with side effects and don't suit everyone, which has driven the search for alternatives. Aromatic plants, from lavender to basil, have long been used to aid relaxation, but it has been hard to pin down which scent molecules actually affect sleep.

A team led by Assistant Professor Zhang Dachuan of the NUS Department of Food Science and Technology set out to find such molecules using a data-driven approach that combines AI with vast plant chemistry data. In the study, featured on the cover of the journal Digital Discovery, the team curated a refined library of 2,391 scent molecules drawn from 991 aromatic plant species, and trained a machine learning model to recognize patterns linked to sleep-promoting activity. The work was done in collaboration with Professor Kou Xingran of the Shanghai Institute of Technology in China.

In testing, the model achieved 96.1% accuracy, largely separating sleep-aiding compounds from those that are not. It also flagged hundreds of plant scent molecules as promising candidates. To see whether the computer's predictions translated into real biological effects, the team selected five commercially available molecules for testing. Of these, four — carvacrol, safranal, vanillin and methyl eugenol — reduced wakefulness and increased the restorative sleep stage known as non-REM sleep.

These molecules also acted on GABA receptors, the brain's main calming signaling system and a well-known target of existing sleep medications. It's an early clue to how certain plant scents engage sleep-related pathways.

Beyond individual molecules, the team also ranked plant families and species rich in promising scent molecules. Among the 991 aromatic plant species analyzed, Asteraceae, Lamiaceae and Lauraceae stood out, and species such as lavender and perilla were flagged for further study.

blocks.cap: AI maps plant compounds

blocks.x: These findings are not a finished sleep product. They're closer to a 'practical map' pointing toward promising directions for future research. The approach shows that AI can speed up the discovery of natural ingredients for health products, functional foods, fragrances and wellness applications.

“Many people link calming plant scents to better sleep, but understanding which molecules play that role and what mechanism drives the effect requires stronger evidence,” Assistant Professor Zhang said. He added that the goal is to turn traditional knowledge into a guide for developing safer, more targeted sleep-related products.
Follow-up research will look at long-term safety, how multiple scent molecules interact when combined, and whether the same effects hold up in broader biological and human studies.

Researchers at the Broad Institute confirmed that it is better to start lab protein evolution not from a natural protein but from a more stable, AI-designed one. The AI-designed scaffold opened up more room for the protease to acquire new mutations.
The team reprogrammed a botulinum neurotoxin protease to target ataxin-2, achieving performance 79 times better than the naturally derived version.
The result shows that generative protein design and directed evolution are not competing tools but ones that complement each other in making therapeutic enzymes.

Researchers at NSF NCAR are building AI weather and climate emulators like CAMulator. They reproduce complex atmospheric models at roughly 350 times lower computational cost, producing subseasonal forecasts for the 2-to-8-week range quickly.
Once trained, the emulator can generate long simulations using only a fraction of the time a supercomputer-based physical model would need.
The research targets the gap between weather forecasting and seasonal climate prediction, particularly the notoriously difficult 2-to-8-week window.

Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) is leading the Genesis Mission project. It aims to build an AI system that autonomously operates the gyrotrons used to heat fusion plasma, along with virtual simulations of the hardware.
The work is part of a U.S. national plan to apply AI to scientific discovery in fusion energy.
Autonomous control of heating hardware is a step toward a future in which AI manages and operates fusion reactors.

Researchers at Tohoku University built an AI-based system. It links a materials database, machine-learning interatomic potentials, large language models, intelligent AI agents, and automated experiments into one continuous feedback loop, which the team calls the 'fourth-plus paradigm.'
Experimental results feed back into refining AI predictions, and repeating this cycle sharply cuts the time needed to find advanced energy materials.
This self-driving lab approach targets the trial-and-error bottleneck that has long persisted in materials science.

UCLA researchers' DeepTimeGate is a physics-informed machine-learning framework that reconstructs images seen through light-scattering media. It pairs a reconstruction neural network, which builds the image, with a second algorithm that checks the result against basic physical laws in real time.

Using physics laws as a safeguard allowed clear images from low-cost cameras without expensive equipment. The researchers believe the approach could also be applied to medical imaging and self-driving car sensing.

Nagoya University researchers combined machine learning and quantum chemistry to search for an efficient blue OLED material. They first trained a model on quantum chemistry calculations for 1,000 molecules, then used that model to screen more than 17,000 candidate compounds.

Having AI narrow the candidates upfront sharply cut heavy computing costs, and the promising emitters it selected were then verified experimentally. The researchers believe this kind of generative screening can speed up the search for new materials considerably.

QEWC, introduced by the researchers, is a quantum machine-learning framework that uses quantum geometry to prevent 'catastrophic forgetting.' Catastrophic forgetting is when a model loses earlier skills while learning a new task.
QEWC anchors learning firmly to the geometry of quantum states. This lets quantum AI learn multiple tasks in sequence while preserving what it has built up along the way.

Researchers used artificial intelligence to analyze 20 years of ocean float data and read a new picture of Atlantic circulation. About 4,000 autonomous Argo profiling floats have kept up observations since the program began, regularly diving to a depth of 2,000 meters and transmitting temperature, salinity, and pressure data by satellite.

blocks.cap: Argo buoys dive to a depth of 2,000 meters and resurface, recording temperature, salinity, and pressure data. Credit: Cristian Clauwers

blocks.x: The study, published in Ocean Science, focuses on the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). The paper describes this circulation as “a vast, conveyor-belt-like system that carries warm surface water northward, where it cools and sinks to great depths, then returns south as cold deep water.”

The researchers trained a machine learning algorithm on high-resolution ocean simulations, combining observational data with model calculations. After having the algorithm learn correlation patterns between currents and temperature-salinity profiles, they applied it to actual Argo observations.

blocks.cap: Workflow for reconstructing the AMOC from Argo profiles. Credit: Ocean Science (2025). DOI: 10.5194/os-21-3541-2025

blocks.x: Lead author Dr. Yannick Wölker said, “Combining machine learning with established physics models lets us draw more out of existing observational data.” The reconstructed circulation estimates matched well with existing observational series and models, proving useful for estimating the strength of large-scale currents from point observations, particularly for measuring the circulation's geostrophic component.

However, the method doesn't adequately capture short-term variability or long-term AMOC weakening. The researchers stressed that the approach “is not meant to replace existing observation systems but to effectively complement and optimize them.” Professor Arne Biastoch said, “AI methods can help make the best possible strategic decisions about future ocean observation.”

This piece examines whether artificial intelligence can read the social dynamics of group work by analyzing nonverbal signals like silence. Research shows that “a group's collective intelligence (CI) rises the more social sensitivity members show and the more evenly they share conversational turns.” But noticing a behavioral pattern isn't the same as understanding what it means.

A 2024 study by Dang and colleagues split 30 Finnish secondary school students into ten teams for a collaborative design task. The students developed food products via voice messages while customer complaints grew increasingly heated. The study revealed three deliberation styles. In elaborated deliberation, silence accounted for about 18% of interactions and mainly appeared during exchanges of learning; in coordinated deliberation, silence served as a transition linking task phases. In isolated deliberation, by contrast, silence dominated about 36% of interactions, which could reflect personal reflection or fragmented group dynamics.

However, AI could only flag patterns of silence, not reveal what the students actually thought or felt. In a 2025 study by Cohn and colleagues, experienced teachers reviewed a dashboard combining video, speech, screen activity, emotion indicators, and engagement. The study distinguished between “difficulty thresholds,” the first signs of struggle, and “intervention points,” where help actually helps. Crucially, the same signal — silence — required different responses depending on context.

The piece notes that “noticing that something happened is different from understanding what it means. A quiet moment could be confusion, frustration, personal focus, or shared reflection.” AI can capture silence down to the millisecond, yet it's clumsy at reading context, and it can mistake reflection for a problem and cut off productive group thinking. The author concludes that “the most socially sensitive AI may not be the one that always knows what to say, but the one that also knows when to stay quiet.”

Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University (OIST) built a virtual robot that used curiosity as a learning signal. It learned language comprehension twice as fast as a robot without curiosity. The study appeared in Science Advances.

blocks.cap: A virtual OIST robot that received curiosity as a learning signal.

blocks.x: The robot used PV-RNN, a brain-inspired predictive coding neural network. The robot rewarded for novel behavior — the curious one — learned language tasks far faster. The gap widened especially on complex, multi-step tasks.

Midway through training, unprompted play appeared. The curious robot “repeatedly experimented with behaviors completely different from what it was instructed to do.” Behavior that was never separately programmed emerged on its own.

The diversity of the language environment also mattered greatly. A robot exposed to 48 verb-adjective-object combinations generalized successfully only 25% of the time, while one exposed to 180 combinations rose to 85%. More varieties of speech improved transfer learning.

The U-shaped curve also appeared. The robot performed well at first, dipped in accuracy while learning a new rule, then climbed back up as it mastered exceptions. The same pattern of overgeneralization seen in toddlers emerged on its own in the model.
The researchers are targeting Chomsky’s “poverty of the stimulus” problem. They believe curiosity and a rich environment can explain why children learn language so quickly despite sparse input.
On Friday, July 11, OpenAI released GPT-5.6 Sol, which solved the cycle double cover conjecture. Several mathematicians proposed it in the 1970s, and it had remained open for more than 50 years.

blocks.cap: An image depicting a graph. Yuichiro Chino/Getty Images

blocks.x: The conjecture states that almost every graph can be covered by cycles so that each edge belongs to exactly two cycles. The AI’s proof shows that, aside from graphs where large clusters connect through only a single edge, any graph can be doubly covered by no more than eight cycles.
The prompt was unusual. It set 64 AI agents working on the problem simultaneously and added one line: “Spend at least eight hours on this before thinking about turning back or giving up.”
Noga Alon of Princeton said it was “another impressive example showing that AI tools will substantially change mathematical research, and already are.”

Andrew Sutherland of MIT said a problem’s reputation for difficulty can itself discourage human attention and become a self-fulfilling prophecy that blocks progress. “I think we’ll keep seeing this — LLMs finding easy solutions to problems that were thought to be hard.” In fact, this proof used almost no new ideas, instead weaving together methods people had already built.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania released PeptiVerse, an open-source AI platform. It calculates a peptide's key properties in advance, before costly, time-consuming synthesis and experiments. The study appeared in Nature Communications (2026).

blocks.cap: A laptop showing the PeptiVerse screen next to peptide synthesis equipment.

blocks.x: A drug candidate has to clear several hurdles. PeptiVerse predicts solubility and cell permeability, toxicity and resistance to protein aggregation, and even bioavailability and how long a compound stays active in the body. The idea is to filter out drug-development bottlenecks computationally, first.
It doesn't predict everything with one model. Each property uses its own tailored machine-learning architecture.

Existing computational tools required programming knowledge to use. PeptiVerse lets users enter a peptide sequence into a web interface and get predictions back as images. First author Yinuo Zhang said, “I wanted researchers to be able to see what's happening inside, not just end up downloading a Python package.”
It also shows the data used in training. Experimentalists can read the predictions alongside molecules whose properties are already known.

Senior author Pranam Chatterjee said it prevents researchers from learning “too late” that a promising-looking molecule ultimately can't become a drug. It doesn't stop at screening, either. It also guides generative AI as it designs new peptides with desired therapeutic properties.
AI is finding therapeutic targets faster than ever. But that speed has exposed the next bottleneck.
Validating predictions requires real experiments, but the lab's physical throughput can't keep up.
The key point is that closing the loop between AI predictions and validated drug candidates requires better-quality experimental data.
Researchers at Rensselaer Polytechnic found that leading AI protein structure prediction tools often produce results that are physically and chemically impossible.
A structure can look plausible yet not hold up as a real molecule. This blind spot stays hidden if the prediction is simply trusted.
The researchers stressed that physics-based molecular dynamics validation and human review remain essential.
A new theoretical framework proposes two scalable quantum circuit designs along with a parallel training method.

The key lies in mathematically avoiding the 'barren plateau.' A barren plateau is a barrier where training signals vanish as circuits grow larger, making large quantum neural networks effectively untrainable.
The researchers aimed to design the structure so it remains trainable while staying hard to simulate on classical computers.

A new computer model is counted among the first AI tools to speed scientific discovery in agriculture and biogeochemistry, with a study finding it 50 times more efficient than earlier models. It is a proof of concept showing that AI can reveal biological processes that are not well understood.

In a paper published in the journal Geoscientific Model Development, the researchers demonstrated the AI by applying it to the problem of soil organic carbon. Earth's soils hold about three-quarters of terrestrial carbon, more than the atmosphere and all the world's plants combined.

Scientists have long looked for ways to use AI in research, but common tools like ChatGPT mostly just reweave existing information. AI has also been used to pull patterns out of data. This model, called a biogeochemistry-informed neural network (BINN), goes a step further, predicting biological processes that are still poorly understood and even surfacing the factors that drive them.

blocks.cap: Diagram of the BINN architecture and training flow. Credit: Geoscientific Model Development (2026)

blocks.x: Yiqi Luo, a professor in Cornell's School of Integrative Plant Science and the study's corresponding author, said, “BINN is very easy to use, so it can spread widely across scientific fields,” adding it is “one of the first tools of this kind to boost scientific research with AI.”

Haodi Xu, a doctoral student in Luo's lab, is a co-first author. The research was carried out in collaboration with the lab of Carla Gomes, a professor of computer science at Cornell's Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science.

Understanding soil carbon processes accurately helps both climate change forecasting and the development of practical solutions, and even small adjustments to this process have large downstream effects. In fact, in 2015 French soil scientists proposed the “4 per 1,000” initiative: the idea that if people adopted practices that raised the world's soil organic carbon in farmland by 0.4% a year, it would, in theory, not only improve soil health but offset all human-made carbon emissions.

How soil gains organic carbon is itself already known. Plants pull carbon from carbon dioxide and lock it in as they grow, and when they die, the organic matter in stems, leaves and roots gradually breaks down into smaller pieces and becomes part of the soil. But scientists don't know well how fast this process runs, or how many steps are needed to break down fallen leaves.
Xu said, “We're using AI and data to quantitatively figure out how fast this process is and how many steps it takes.”

BINN computed 50 times faster than earlier models. Its accuracy in predicting soil organic carbon levels was very close to that of existing models. However, existing models carried a spatial bias, favoring data from one region over another when predicting across the U.S. mainland. The researchers confirmed that BINN showed less of this spatial bias.

blocks.cap: Spatial map of normalized differences between BINN and PRODA. Credit: Geoscientific Model Development (2026)

blocks.x: The researchers say the model can also be adapted to illuminate other poorly understood agricultural and biogeochemical processes, such as soil respiration or carbon accumulation in forest ecosystems.

A KAIST research team has introduced a next-generation world model that learns executable theories purely from observation. A world model refers to the internal model an AI builds on its own to understand and predict the world.

Led by professor Sung-Jin Ahn of the School of Computing, the team proposed a new learning paradigm called Learning-to-Theorize (L2T), which trains AI to theorize about how the world works using only observed information. They also built a neural network model that implements it, called the Neural Theorizer (NEO).

The research was presented at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), held in Seoul from July 6 to 11. The paper, posted on the arXiv preprint server, was selected as the best paper at the Compositional Learning workshop.

blocks.cap: Overview of the Learning-to-Theorize (L2T) framework.

blocks.x: World models are a foundational technology spanning robot control, autonomous driving, generative AI, and autonomous agents that judge and act on their own. Until now, the focus has been on predicting what happens next. Even when a model predicted a scene accurately, it did not necessarily understand why the change happened or the principles governing the world.

The team found a clue in how people learn. Children build their own theories about how the world works long before they learn to speak. Applying this view from developmental cognitive science to AI, the team built a system that understands the principles of change instead of simply predicting the future.

L2T does not provide correct answers or rules in advance. Given only “before the change” and “after the change” observations, the AI figures out on its own which rule produced that change. Unlike existing methods that focus on guessing the next scene, it is designed to understand why the change happened.

NEO finds reusable basic units, or primitives, hidden within observed transformations and assembles them into executable programs. These learned primitives can then be systematically recombined to explain new situations.

For example, NEO learns on its own units corresponding to basic operations like rotation, moving left or down, and coloring. Even when it encounters a combination never seen in training, such as “move down, then color, then rotate,” it recombines the units it has already learned to explain and solve that situation.

Existing AI, by contrast, memorizes entangled patterns as a single lump, so its performance drops sharply when it meets an unfamiliar combination. The team showed in multiple experiments that NEO outperforms existing approaches in compositional generalization, the ability to combine learned basic rules to solve problems it has never seen before.

Professor Ahn said, “This points to a new direction beyond prediction-focused world models, what we call a World Theory Model,” adding, “We expect it to develop into a core technology across fields such as intelligent robotics, autonomous agents, and AI that aids scientific discovery.”
Master's students Doo-Jin Baek and Gyu-Bin Lee of the School of Computing participated as co-first authors.

Language-based history-taking alone can elicit a substantial share of clinical diagnoses. Face-to-face and telehealth visits between doctor and patient remain the standard here, but access is often limited by cost, geography and institutional barriers. Google Research researchers ran a large-scale study examining whether a conversational AI agent could handle everything from symptom intake to differential diagnosis on its own.

The paper, “SymptomAI: Towards a Conversational AI Agent for Everyday Symptom Assessment,” reports results from a nationwide randomized study (n=13,917). Consenting participants spoke with one of five SymptomAI agents built on Gemini Flash 2.0. The diagnoses and labels produced during the study are for research analysis only, not confirmed clinical diagnoses.

blocks.cap: Screen from the SymptomAI research app showing symptom intake and a diagnosis summary.

blocks.x: Participants described their symptoms and SymptomAI asked follow-up questions, with each conversation ending in a differential diagnosis (DDx) list and next-step recommendations. Participants later reported the outcome of any clinician visit in a survey two weeks afterward. For evaluation, a panel of three specialist physicians reviewed the conversation transcripts, each producing their own differential diagnosis, and then ranked SymptomAI's diagnoses against other clinicians' under blinded conditions.

Clinicians preferred SymptomAI's differential diagnosis over another clinician's in more than half of cases. On top-5 accuracy, which checks whether a participant's actual diagnosis from their treating physician appeared among five candidates, clinicians also rated SymptomAI's diagnoses as correct more often than their peers'.

blocks.cap: SymptomAI was preferred more often as the top-ranked best diagnosis, at 53.3%.

blocks.x: Participants were split into five arms that received different questioning strategies. Every strategy in which SymptomAI actively asked follow-up questions clearly outperformed the baseline condition corresponding to today's user-led chatbot approach. SymptomAI's edge was largest in cases where clinicians were least confident in their own diagnosis.

The researchers also compared SymptomAI's diagnoses with participants' Fitbit wearable biosignals recorded before the conversation. Conversations that led to infectious-disease diagnoses overlapped with physiological changes suggestive of an immune response, with clear shifts in cardiovascular function, respiration, skin temperature and sleep quality appearing days before symptoms were reported.

Still, differential diagnosis itself is an inherently ambiguous task, and diagnoses can change over time. In the evaluation, clinicians saw only static conversation transcripts and couldn't ask their own follow-up questions, and the setup carries the further limitation that signals like body language, visual examination or medical records could be missed.

Researchers at Triplebar Bio, UC Berkeley, and BioMADE are developing an AI model for cell engineering tailored to bioproduction environments. Triplebar Bio CEO Shawn Manchester said the key question is “figuring out how to modify a host cell's genome to get the best performance in bioproduction.”

The core of the project is generating data under conditions close to actual production, and doing so at scale. Manchester said what sets it apart is “the ability to pull data at the scale of hundreds of thousands of cells and data points, in an environment that mirrors bioproduction.”

blocks.cap: Researchers at Triplebar Bio holding a droplet microfluidics chip.

blocks.x: The research uses Pichia pastoris as the host cell to produce five proteins used in bioprocessing. The method weaves together two strands. One is droplet microfluidics technology, which traps cells in water-oil emulsion droplets and measures protein output with fluorescent sensors. The other is a multimodal transformer-based AI model, which analyzes sequencing data from high- and low-performing cells to find correlations between genotype and phenotype.

Training proceeds by first pretraining on thousands of genomes, then fine-tuning on genotype-phenotype data specific to bioproduction. Manchester said he expects “more than 10% of designs to lead to meaningful improvement,” a far higher rate than the traditional design-build-test cycle manages in its early stages.
The ultimate goal is for a company to input its own production conditions and have the AI output a genetic design that boosts strain performance.

Large language models (LLMs) are gradually reshaping life-science research. The shift goes beyond boosting productivity, and it's hardening into a new standard before scientists have even agreed on how far its use should go.

A paper by an international team of researchers, published in Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment, calls this the 'creeping normalization' of generative AI: a phenomenon where large changes happen in small, subtle steps until they're accepted almost without notice. Lead author Ivan Jarić of the Biology Centre of the Czech Academy of Sciences said, “Generative AI has already entered the daily work of many researchers, but its long-term impact across nearly every area of science has received relatively little attention,” adding, “habitually relying on this tool could fundamentally change the foundations of scientific practice and culture.”

blocks.cap: A diagram proposing how far it is appropriate to allow AI at each stage of the scientific process. Source: Ivan Jarić

blocks.x: The paper points to areas where change is already visible. One is collaboration. Researchers are increasingly handing off tasks like bouncing around ideas, working through analytical problems, or seeking expert opinion to LLMs instead of colleagues. The more this happens, the less incentive there is to seek out expertise from other fields or regions, weakening interdisciplinary exchange and narrowing the diversity of perspectives.

How people search for information and get ideas is also changing. Susan Canavan of the University of Galway said that as LLMs take over the role of search engines, encyclopedias, and literature review, “you become locked into only the questions you thought to ask, and more dependent on the answers the AI gives you.” That, she said, can entrench confirmation bias, create intellectual echo chambers, and homogenize scientific language and ideas.

There's also the problem of core skills dulling. Foundational abilities like literature review and synthesis, taxonomic judgment, and coding and statistical reasoning are being handed over to LLMs. That could reduce the need to open new PhD and postdoc positions, affecting hiring and career paths as well.

Michael Bertram of the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences said, “Rather than being for or against AI, let's set boundaries for what counts as appropriate use.” He argued it's fine to use AI widely for routine tasks like proofreading or polishing language, but that it's not advisable for roles requiring independent scientific judgment, such as setting research priorities, peer review, funding decisions, or ethical judgment. The researchers conclude that a generative-AI-driven transformation of science is already underway, and the real question isn't whether AI will enter research, but where the community draws the line.

A material's properties arise from interactions among countless atoms. Simulating each of those atoms individually, especially over long timescales, is usually impossible even for today's supercomputers. Whether the goal is an energy-efficient electronic device or a new alloy, design starts from understanding macroscopic material behavior, and that's exactly where the computational bottleneck sits.

A research team led by Associate Professor Qianxiao Li in the Department of Mathematics at the National University of Singapore (NUS) has introduced an AI method to get around this wall. Instead of tracking particles one by one, it finds a handful of hidden variables that capture the collective behavior of the whole system and predicts how their values change over time. The results appeared in a Physical Review Materials paper and a separate paper presented at ICML 2026.

blocks.cap: A method that trains on data from a small system to predict the macroscopic behavior of a much larger one. Source: National University of Singapore

blocks.x: The first result is a method that accurately predicts the behavior of a much larger stochastic system using only simulations of a small one. Instead of computing the forces on every atom in the large system, it learns how the whole thing moves from force information on only some of the atoms. The team proved mathematically that this shortcut still leads to an accurate model, and validated it on everything from biological population models to simulated alloys with more than 500,000 atoms.

The second result handles systems where the microscopic components have no fixed order, such as fluids, particle ensembles, and polymers. Rather than tracking particles one by one, it learns the overall pattern of the distribution, so the result is the same no matter how the particles are numbered.

The key advantage is scalability. Because the method can infer the behavior of systems far larger than what it was trained on, it opens a path to handling real materials at scales that had been difficult to touch. Professor Li said the goal is “to build AI that automatically discovers how macroscopic behavior emerges from countless microscopic interactions,” while sharply cutting computational cost and preserving physical accuracy. The team is preparing the next step: connecting this method to experimental data, particularly simulations of mid-sized materials.

AI models have become everyday tools that anyone can use, and scientists across fields have started using them to assist research and experiments. Researchers at Stanford University and the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory tried using an AI agent to prepare a synchrotron X-ray experiment. A synchrotron is a large facility that accelerates electrons to produce extremely bright X-rays, used to examine the atomic structure of materials, molecules, and biological samples.

In a paper published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the researchers had the agent prepare an actual synchrotron experiment. The agent planned its own actions, interpreted observations, generated instrument-control commands, and completed sample alignment.

blocks.cap: The operating flow of the agentic X-ray scientist. It reads detector images, experiment logs, and scan results, judges the state, and issues instrument-control commands. Source: Chen et al., Nature Machine Intelligence (2026)

blocks.x: First author Zhantao Chen said, “We demonstrated an agentic AI X-ray scientist that aligns a single-crystal sample on a synchrotron beamline by itself.” Sample alignment is the first step in nearly every single-crystal experiment, yet it's labor-intensive and tedious. He explained that the agent asks about the state of the experiment, judges what's happening and what to do next, and pushes through to alignment.

The agent is given a toolkit that includes reading experiment logs, capturing detector images, and running motor scans. Chen said, “If you want it to tighten a screw, you have to give it a screwdriver along with instructions on how to use it,” explaining that the tools connect the AI to the actual experiment while the prompts teach it how to use those tools well. He said this flexibility, responding quickly when conditions change or new information comes in, is the strength of LLM-based agents. Traditional automation would require countless hand-coded conditional branches for every situation.

blocks.cap: A Co₃Sn₂S₂ single-crystal sample mounted on a copper holder, and the six-circle diffractometer at the SSRL BL17-2 beamline where the demonstration took place. Source: Chen et al., Nature Machine Intelligence (2026)

blocks.x: The key was a virtual beamline the researchers built. Large facilities are always booked solid, making it hard to develop directly on real equipment from scratch. After completing the whole workflow in the simulator, they made only small tweaks to the input and output formats and moved it to the real beamline, where it worked as is. Chen said this approach could extend to other experimental tasks, and that the team is developing a more general agent framework for use across materials science and physics labs, beyond X-ray beamlines.

Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made remarkable progress in restoring movement and speech for patients with paralysis. Until now, BCIs have mostly focused on decoding motor function, but depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder, the conditions with the heaviest brain-disease burden, are fundamentally problems of cognition, such as attention, memory, judgment and emotion regulation. A new review points out that treating cognitive disorders requires an approach entirely different from today's motor-focused BCIs.

Dr. Ignacio Saez, director of the Human Neurophysiology Research Laboratory at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, outlined a roadmap for a next-generation 「cognitive brain-computer interface」 in a commentary published in Trends in Cognitive Sciences. Decoding thought is entirely different from decoding movement. Movement is encoded in small, stable brain regions, but the activity underlying attention, memory and emotion is spread across multiple regions and takes place in networks that reorganize from moment to moment. That is why the same signal can mean different things depending on context.

Dr. Saez said, 「BCIs have made remarkable progress in restoring movement and speech, and I believe we are at an inflection point,」 adding that a path is opening up to target cognitive function. The review emphasizes that technologies for reading the brain and stimulating it need to be merged into a single closed-loop system.

Such a system would need to catch the moment an abnormal brain state appears and respond with precisely tailored adaptive neurostimulation. The necessary pieces, such as intracranial brain recording, adaptive neurostimulation and high-resolution neurochemical sensing, already exist in clinical and research settings. Weaving them into an intelligent closed loop is the next task, and it could open the way to more precise, personalized treatment for serious brain disorders.

This shift toward cognition coincides with growing commercial interest. Companies that have led motor and speech BCIs see cognitive applications as the next frontier, since the patient population for depression, anxiety, PTSD and similar conditions is far larger than for paralysis. Dr. Saez noted that moving lab results into approved treatments will require academia, clinics and industry to jointly build the hardware, algorithms and regulatory pathways.

Deep learning has changed how scientists predict the activity and function of DNA sequences in the genome. Corgi (Context-aware Regulatory Genomics Inference), developed by the Martin Vingron Bioinformatics Group at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics, predicts how the genome behaves differently across cell types. The achievement contributes to efforts to virtually simulate cell activity, and has potential applications in basic research and medicine.

Cells in the body may look similar, but small genetic variants make each person's genetic makeup different. These variants alter gene expression in cells and draw interest because they can be tied to disease mechanisms or offer clues for personalized treatment. Yet only a handful of these variants turn out to be functionally meaningful.

Many existing tools had a fundamental limitation: they could not account for the cellular context that switches genes on and off, so they failed to generalize beyond their training data. Ekin Deniz Aksu, first author of the paper published in Nature Communications, said, 「With Corgi, we have overcome much of this limitation. It properly predicts measurements tied to genome activity, such as gene expression, chromatin accessibility and histone modification.」

Earlier models largely ignored cellular context and relied only on sequence. But DNA does not act alone; it works together with numerous regulatory molecules. That is why the same sequence behaves differently in a neuron than in a liver cell. Aksu explained, 「We integrated large amounts of expression data from regulatory genes to build a structure that is closer to actual cell biology.」

The improved Corgi+ infers epigenetic information from RNA sequencing data. With further refinement, it could fill data gaps in settings where running every experiment directly is difficult, such as rare cells, embryos and small-quantity patient tissue.

The researchers hope this approach will also improve virtual cell models. Virtual cells simulate the effects of genetic perturbation at the cell level but do not capture information on DNA activity. Aksu said, 「Going forward, our model could help bridge sequence-to-function models with virtual cells.」 Such systems could also be used to virtually screen drug candidates and to understand how mutations alter cellular processes to cause complex diseases.

Picture a symphony orchestra playing a complex masterpiece. If the violins drifted out of tune every few bars, the orchestra would have to keep stopping to retune. Fortunately, that never happens with a real orchestra. Yet that's exactly the reality of running a quantum computer today.

A quantum computer is, at its core, an analog machine sensitive to drift. To run stably, the frequency, amplitude, and phase of the analog signals that direct the qubits must be constantly readjusted. Today, that can only be done by completely halting the computation. For useful quantum algorithms that need to run for days or months, this is a fundamental bottleneck.

In a paper published in Nature, “Reinforcement learning control of quantum error correction,” Google presented a reinforcement learning (RL) framework in which an autonomous agent learns from quantum error detection to steer thousands of control variables in real time. In effect, it found a way to tune the instruments while the performance keeps going.

blocks.cap: QEC extending the lifetime of logical information in quantum memory based on the surface code (left) and the color code (right). Credit: Google Research

blocks.x: Quantum error correction (QEC) builds a 'logical qubit' out of multiple physical qubits and uses parity checks to turn analog noise into binary error-detection signals. However, this signal only tells you that an error occurred somewhere in a given region of spacetime in the circuit, not its exact location. Neural-network decoders like AlphaQubit and algorithmic decoders like Tesseract estimate where the error occurred to recover the information.

Google validated this RL control on its flagship superconducting processor, Willow. In experiments that deliberately introduced artificial drift into the control variables, RL steering boosted the logical stability of the error-correcting code by 3.5 times. Even after careful hand calibration by experts, RL fine-tuning lowered the logical error rate by another 20%.
This experiment cut logical errors to record levels, less than once per thousand error-correction cycles for the surface code, and about once per hundred for the color code.

In simulations run with hundreds of qubits and tens of thousands of control variables, the number of RL training iterations needed didn't depend on system size. This opens a new path toward quantum computers that keep correcting errors without stopping, and learn on their own.

Researchers at Duke University School of Medicine have built an AI framework that redesigns proteins on a scale you'd otherwise only see in natural evolution. It produces shorter, longer, or substantially altered variants while keeping the structure and function intact.

It's called Raygun. Instead of drawing up a protein from scratch, it broadly reworks existing proteins on top of a protein language model trained on millions of natural protein sequences. The research was published in Nature.

“There's a language that governs how a protein's amino acid sequence leads to shape and function, but scientists don't yet fully understand that language,” said co-corresponding author Assistant Professor Rohit Singh. “A protein language model, like a translator, learns patterns from millions of sequences and connects them to biological structure and function.”

Raygun adds a new way of representing proteins on top of this. Rather than treating them only as amino acid chains of varying length, it converts them into a standard formula format that holds the core patterns the AI has learned. Since proteins of any size are expressed in the same format, they can be compared, shortened, or lengthened for redesign.

blocks.cap: Researchers in a lab at Duke University School of Medicine. Credit: Eamon Queeney / Duke University School of Medicine

blocks.x: Researchers tune Raygun with just two settings. One controls how much the sequence changes, and the other decides whether the protein is made shorter or longer.

Across multiple experiments, the AI-designed proteins retained their predicted structural stability and key functional regions. Live-cell experiments confirmed this with fluorescent proteins used for imaging and enzymes that carry out essential cellular tasks, while receptor-binding experiments validated variants of epidermal growth factor (EGF), which is involved in wound healing and tied to signaling pathways linked to cancer.
This approach helps researchers design tools for gene therapy, biotechnology, and biomedical research more efficiently. At the same time, it offers new clues about how proteins evolve in nature.

The IMDEA Materials Institute has introduced an acoustic imaging technique that overcomes a fundamental limitation of technologies like ultrasound imaging. It reconstructs a complete, accurate image using only the signal a single fixed sensor captures in one instant, with no need for an array of multiple sensors or long scan times.

Conventional acoustic imaging required either a probe with multiple transducers — that is, a sensor array — capturing signals from different positions at once, or a single sensor taking multiple measurements while moving. “Traditional methods come with considerable complexity, cost, and equipment size,” explained Johan Christensen, principal investigator at IMDEA Materials. “Our new method solves this by packing all of an object's spatial information into the frequency spectrum of a single sound.”

blocks.cap: How a single-signal acoustic image is made using an AI-synthesized frequency codec. Credit: IMDEA Materials Institute

blocks.x: The method, published in Advanced Functional Materials, fires a single broadband ultrasonic pulse at an object. The scattered wave carrying the object's shape information passes through an inexpensive 'disordered medium.' In the experiment, this medium was a sheet of agar embedded with randomly placed steel beads, acting as a physical encoder. Its irregular structure makes the path differ slightly for each frequency component, producing a unique spectral 'fingerprint' that a single sensor captures.

To the human eye it's unrecognizable, but this fingerprint contains all the information needed to reconstruct the image. The researchers trained a neural network to act as the decoder. Once trained, the AI interprets the incoming signal and restores an image of the original object in tens of microseconds. In an experiment reconstructing handwritten digits engraved on a metal plate, it achieved up to 98.7% structural similarity with the original.

The technology opens the way to ultra-compact, low-cost, real-time acoustic imaging devices. Its applications range widely, from medical diagnostics that image moving organs like a beating heart with much simpler equipment, to industrial non-destructive testing and underwater object detection. The researchers believe the principle is universal enough to extend to 3D imaging or other types of waves. The study was an international collaboration between Nanjing University, Nanjing Forestry University, and Wuhan Polytechnic University (China), together with the IMDEA Materials Institute.

Hospitals adopted AI note-writing tools quickly. The rationale was less physician burnout and higher revenue. But medical schools face a different question: should students and trainees use AI scribes that generate clinical notes automatically? A STAT News article covered how schools and hospitals are divided over this question.

blocks.cap: Credit: Adobe Stock

blocks.x: Educators' worry is clear. If students stop writing differential diagnoses themselves, the cognitive struggle that builds diagnostic reasoning disappears too. The push to train a workforce comfortable with technology collides head-on with the worry that thinking should not be outsourced while learning habits are still forming.

Jaideep Talwalkar, associate dean for educational technology and innovation at Yale School of Medicine, says: “The deliberate process of creating a note forces us to use our heads to wrestle with what's happening right now. There's value in repeating that many, many times.”

For now, schools and hospitals are limiting trainee access while waiting for better research. It is a question every field that automates paperwork will soon face. Building expertise is, in the end, productive struggle — so if a machine takes over that struggle, where does skill grow? (The STAT+ article is for subscribers only; the full text is not public.)

A team at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab), under the U.S. Department of Energy, has unveiled an AI modeling technique that quickly and accurately foresees how reactions between solid materials unfold over time. It is the first predictive model to also account for how atoms move through the material as a reaction proceeds. Above all, the prediction translates directly into an optimal recipe for making advanced materials.

blocks.cap: The reaction interface where an A-cation-rich precursor (α) meets a B-cation-rich precursor (β) to form the intermediate phase γ. Credit: Nature Materials (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5

blocks.x: “Thanks to the new model, materials scientists and industry can make promising new materials much faster, with higher purity and yield,” says Kristin Persson, one of the paper's authors. She is a senior scientist at Berkeley Lab and a professor in the materials science and engineering department at UC Berkeley. “This model speeds up how quickly solid materials move toward cheap manufacturing and commercialization. It bridges the gap between materials discovery and new technology.” The study was published in Nature Materials.

Next-generation technologies like batteries, sensors and medical devices rely on inorganic solid materials that store energy, emit light and catalyze reactions. AI computational tools have already made it possible to pick out materials with the desired properties. The problem is what comes next. Powder mixing and high-temperature heating, the common way to make inorganic solids, often produce an unexpected jumble of compounds instead of the intended product. Finding the right recipe can take weeks to years of trial and error.

Existing computational models forecast outcomes using thermodynamics, weighing which reactions are energetically favorable and which products are stable. “Thermodynamics tells you how much two solids ‘want’ to react with each other,” Persson explains. But the predictions didn't hold up well, because they left out kinetics — how atoms move around while the reaction proceeds. “Atoms in a solid move more slowly than in a liquid, so it's hard for them to reach the reaction site. No matter how much two materials want to react, if enough atoms can't get there, the reaction simply doesn't happen.” That's also why solid-state reactions require heating up to 800°C (1,470°F) — to get atoms moving.

On top of thermodynamics, the team added a machine-learning model trained to predict how fast atoms move through a material. The design grew out of the hypothesis that the reaction interface between two solids is extremely disordered. “Picture the chaos of a crowd rushing out of a stadium all at once after a big show ends — that's exactly what the atoms at the reaction site look like.” Fed the starting materials, their ratios and a temperature ramp, the model simulates the reaction from start to finish in minutes, showing intermediate products, final products and even impurities.

The test case was barium-titanium oxide, widely used in electronics. “We chose it deliberately because the reaction depends heavily on kinetics. When you heat powders containing barium and titanium, the compounds that newly form have almost identical thermodynamic stability. Since they all equally ‘want’ to form, what decides the outcome is how easily atoms can reach the reaction interface.” The model's simulated results matched decades' worth of synthesis data from the literature. “It was striking that the entire sequence of events — intermediate compounds, final products, even impurity formation — matched up.” The team plans to extend the training to other material families, eventually building a foundation model from a large-scale kinetics dataset.

On May 20, 2026, OpenAI shook the mathematics world. The announcement was that an undisclosed internal model had found a counterexample to the “unit distance” problem — a conjecture posed in 1946 by the itinerant Hungarian mathematician Paul Erdős. The explanation was simple but mathematically deep, and it was the first AI-derived proof significant enough to make history. On August 1, OpenAI said an undisclosed model called Astra had made ten pieces of progress, including on three Erdős problems.

blocks.cap: Paul Erdős, one of the most prolific mathematicians in history. Credit: Photo by George Csicsery from the documentary N is a Number: A Portrait of Paul Erdős ©1993

blocks.x: “This trend is dramatically changing how mathematical research is done,” says Noga Alon of Princeton University, who has solved dozens of Erdős problems over his career. Erdős lived out of a single suitcase, drifting between friends' homes, pouring problems into papers and letters and offering his own money as a prize to whoever solved them first.

It started with British mathematician Thomas Bloom. Finding it hard to track what had been solved and what had been forgotten, he gathered the problems and launched erdosproblems.com in early 2023. He wrote the Python code running the site with ChatGPT. Over 2024 and the first eight months of 2025, 111 problems moved from “open” to “solved.” When comments were added in August 2025, a community formed. When Wouter van Doorn, who works at a consulting firm, posted progress he'd made without AI, a user pointed out a flaw — and after the back-and-forth, the one who backed down was Terence Tao of UCLA.

blocks.cap: Thomas Bloom's Erdős problems site became a gathering place for the best of mathematics. Then AI showed up. Credit: Courtesy of Thomas Bloom

blocks.x: Kevin Barreto and Liam Price, both in their early twenties, started throwing problems in bulk at the latest models in December. Noticing that GPT-5.2 made little headway when told a problem's answer was unknown, they crafted prompts that “make it believe the problem is easier than it really is.” Problem 728, solved with GPT-5.2 Pro on January 4, 2026, had no prior research behind it.

Erdős problems tend to fall first mainly because most belong to number theory, combinatorics and graph theory — areas large language models handle relatively well. Bloom points to a different worry: “A lot of people using AI can't verify the output. It's like, 'AI generated the proof, checked it, and even wrote the paper' — and nobody has read it, and nobody is going to.”

blocks.cap: Terence Tao first met Erdős when he was ten years old. Credit: Billy Grace Tao

blocks.x: In January, a team of 24 researchers led by Google DeepMind used Gemini to sweep through 700 “open” conjectures, solving four problems and recovering nine forgotten solutions. In May, a separate 21-person DeepMind team announced that “our best agent autonomously solved 9 of 353 open problems, at a cost of a few hundred dollars per problem.” Cambridge's Tim Gowers wrote of the OpenAI solution that “if a human had submitted this paper to the Annals of Mathematics, I would have had no hesitation in recommending it for publication.” The original paper simply listed its author as “OpenAI.”

Alon has now stepped back. “Once AI started solving them, it stopped being meaningful,” he says. Tao, too, has withdrawn from the community. Van Doorn still works at his firm: “Someone who wants to play the piano doesn't hire a machine that plays better than they do.” In July 2026, on the very day the Fields Medal winners were announced, Jacob Tsimerman said he was leaving academia to join OpenAI.

Deciding what to observe, when, and in which direction has long been a human job. This study, a collaboration between Northwestern University, the University of Chicago, and Fermilab, handed that judgment to a reinforcement-learning AI.

The AI builds the Dark Energy Camera's observing schedule on its own. As sky conditions and weather shift moment to moment, it revises the plan in real time, moving on to the next observation without a person adjusting it by hand.

The researchers say the AI's performance rivals that of an experienced human scheduler. It's a milestone on the road to a self-operating observatory, and a case where AI directly advances observational astronomy.

Brain-wave recordings taken during sleep carry a full record of brain health. UCSF researchers used machine learning to analyze overnight sleep EEG from about 7,000 adults and estimate each person's 'brain age.'
The key was the gap between this brain age and actual age. People whose brains looked older than their real age later faced a markedly higher risk of dementia.
It suggests that ordinary sleep-test data could become an early marker of neurological change. The researchers expect this AI biomarker to offer a lead on spotting dementia ahead of time.

When someone raises an unsolved problem, people now check first whether GPT can solve it. That's how a long-standing puzzle around unclonable encryption in quantum cryptography got solved. Two research teams, using the same AI model, produced answers side by side within hours of each other.

blocks.cap: AI pioneer John McCarthy at the blackboard. Today AI has started helping with mathematical proofs

blocks.x: MIT PhD student Seyoon Raghavan assembled the proof by handing the system two-hour chunks of work at a time, checking progress along the way and resetting direction as needed. Prabhanjan Ananth of UC Santa Barbara and Amit Sahai of UCLA used a UCLA-built system that helps the model propose solutions and critique itself. All three used GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra.

Ananth and Sahai posted their paper to arXiv at 10:35 a.m. Pacific time, and Raghavan posted his 3 hours and 18 minutes later. Both papers credit GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra for the core idea. The problem was raised in early July at the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing, and neither paper has gone through peer review yet.

“The general vibe now is this,” Ananth said. “When someone states an unsolved problem, the first thing people do is check whether GPT can solve it.” There are also voices worried about access. Broadbent said, “It raises a lot of questions about the haves and have-nots.”

Watching a large reasoning model get an answer right has become familiar by now. The unresolved question is whether the model is actually reasoning, or just taking a shortcut that looks like reasoning.

blocks.cap: Illustration: Celsius Pictor for Quanta Magazine

blocks.x: The evidence on the skeptical side keeps piling up. Apple researchers' 2025 paper, ‘Illusion of Thinking,’ documented accuracy collapsing wholesale once conditions got only slightly harder. Melanie Mitchell of the Santa Fe Institute concluded that models use surface-level shortcuts on puzzles like ARC-AGI.

A team led by Subbarao Kambhampati at Arizona State University found that swapping a correct reasoning process for a wrong or irrelevant one didn't hurt performance. In a 2024 NYU study, meaningless tokens consisting of nothing but periods served the same role as a reasoning chain, and researchers at Northeastern University and UC Berkeley calculated that 30 to 60 percent of reasoning steps had almost no effect on the final answer.

The other side points to results of its own. In May 2026, OpenAI solved the long-standing unit-distance problem, and Google DeepMind and Terence Tao used AI to recover or improve answers to 67 problems spanning analysis, combinatorics, geometry, and number theory. Performances at the level of International Mathematical Olympiad gold medals have also appeared.

blocks.cap: Illustration: Celsius Pictor for Quanta Magazine

blocks.x: “A fake theory is worse than admitting you have no theory,” Kambhampati said flatly. Whether the reasoning sentences shown on the surface actually mirror the real computation underneath remains an open question.

Researchers from Meta AI, Paris's PSL University, and the Adolphe de Rothschild Foundation Hospital unveiled a system that converts brain signals into sentences without surgery. The goal is to help patients who have lost speech to paralysis or language disorders communicate through a computer.

blocks.cap: EEG and MEG record signals while a participant types a sentence, viewing it one word at a time

blocks.x: The core is a three-stage model called Brain2Qwerty. A convolutional module first processes signals in 500-millisecond windows, a transformer module then learns at the sentence level, and a pretrained language model refines the result and corrects errors.

blocks.cap: The three-stage structure of Brain2Qwerty

blocks.x: Researchers had 35 healthy volunteers type out memorized sentences while recording their brain activity throughout. The character error rate averaged 29% with MEG, which measures magnetic fields, and 65% with EEG, which measures electrical signals. The best-performing participant got the rate down to 18%, and in some cases decoded unfamiliar sentences perfectly.

Researchers Yarod Levy and Mingfang Zhang cautioned that the work has so far only involved healthy people, and that it would need further refinement before use with actual patients. The team wrote in the paper that “these results narrow the gap between invasive and non-invasive approaches, opening a path toward safe brain-computer interfaces for patients who cannot speak.” The paper was published in the journal Nature Neuroscience.

AI chatbots built for clinical settings keep pouring out, but a debate has broken out over whether doctors should trust them. A study NYU Langone Health researchers published in Nature Medicine in June 2026 lit the fuse.

blocks.cap: Large language models enter the clinic (Camille MacMillin/STAT)

blocks.x: Researchers tested general-purpose and medicine-specific models side by side using three sets of clinical questions. OpenEvidence and UpToDate Expert AI were among the specialized models. The result ran against conventional wisdom: models built specifically for medicine actually scored lower than big tech's general-purpose large language models.
A Kaiser Permanente vice president wrote on LinkedIn, “I've never seen a single paper shake up the health AI industry this much.”

Turning ordinary carbon dioxide into valuable fuel requires quickly figuring out which catalyst holds up the longest and most efficiently. AI models can help with that screening, but just like an internet chatbot, a model is only as good as the data fed into it.

Researchers at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory brought together four labs across the country to test an experimental catalyst that produces carbon monoxide, the first step in converting carbon dioxide into fuel. The results, published in Nature Catalysis, show why highly reproducible experimental data matters when building AI models for scientific research.

blocks.cap: The study, conducted across four labs nationwide, shows that standardizing experimental protocols and equipment governs how much results vary. Credit: Adam Hoffman and Greg Stewart/SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory

blocks.x: "It's a cautionary tale about what information you feed into a machine learning model, and how the consistency of experimental data governs the reliability of the results," says Selin Bac, a postdoctoral researcher at UC Santa Barbara and the paper's first author.

With a good model, you can feed in conditions like temperature, reaction time, and catalyst composition, get a performance prediction, and confirm it with a handful of well-designed experiments. That speeds up how fast catalysts get discovered and deployed. Beyond saving time and money, it also lets you examine conditions that are hard to recreate in a lab. Catalyst research usually looks at timescales of just days, but catalyst deactivation, which happens as impurities build up and from repeated exposure to high heat, unfolds over months to years.

Training an AI model requires large amounts of high-quality data. To generate that data, the four labs ran round-robin experiments using a pre-agreed protocol and the same rhodium-based catalyst, a method where multiple labs run the same test to measure reproducibility.

But getting the same result out of four independently working labs turned out to be far harder than expected. When they compared notes, the amounts of carbon monoxide the four teams produced, and of methane, an unwanted byproduct, varied widely. A computer can't learn from four sets of data that don't agree with each other.

"It was an eye-opening experience," said Adam Hoffman, a SLAC researcher and the paper's senior author. "It revealed just how tricky it is in practice to feed real-world data into a machine learning model."

The team took the method apart piece by piece. The causes of the mismatch narrowed down to a handful of factors, with how vigorously the mixture was shaken or stirred contributing the most to the variance. Once researchers from SLAC, along with Penn State, Stanford, and UC Santa Barbara, standardized the procedure further, the results started lining up. The team put together recommendations for improving consistency in reactor design, operating protocols, and experimental conditions.

Hoffman said he hopes the study gets both experimentalists and data scientists thinking about how small design differences between labs can turn into reproducibility problems, and eventually into long-term prediction errors in AI models. "We hope it serves as a guide for how to design experiments meant to go into a machine learning model."

There's no one-size-fits-all approach to designing AI that helps diagnose disease. A new study by MIT and other researchers found that AI assistance generally raised diagnostic accuracy for skin conditions among both laypeople and clinicians, but the effect of explainability techniques depended on the user's level of knowledge.

blocks.cap: A clinician reviewing a skin condition image. In the MIT study, laypeople tended to trust the AI's diagnostic advice even when it was wrong, while clinicians caught errors more often. Credit: iStock

blocks.x: Explainable AI shows the reasoning behind a model's judgment, helping users decide when to trust it—whether by highlighting diagnostically important regions of an image as a heatmap, or having a large language model spell out its prediction in plain language. The researchers compared skin-condition diagnoses by laypeople and primary care physicians, with and without these tools.

Laypeople's accuracy improved, but mostly because they leaned on the AI. They believed LLM explanations whether right or wrong, and the vaguer and more generic an explanation was, the more persuasive they found it. Clinicians, by contrast, were not swayed by flawed AI assistance, and did best when given predictions alone, without explanations.

“Good AI systems can boost performance in some medical settings, but that must be carefully weighed against algorithmic compliance that leads to more errors. Both AI and explanation methods can trigger people's automation bias, and this anchoring effect has to be accounted for when designing these systems,” said Marzyeh Ghassemi, associate professor in MIT's Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a member of the Institute for Medical Engineering and Science, the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and the Jameel Clinic.

Co-author Roxana Daneshjou, assistant professor of biomedical data science and dermatology at Stanford University, noted that patients increasingly turn to AI with health questions, and that people with the least medical knowledge are most easily swayed by explainable AI's wrong outputs.

First author Orson Xu, assistant professor of biomedical informatics at Columbia University, believes the gap comes from how explanations are used. Clinicians already have a diagnosis in mind and check the AI against their own training, so sloppy explanations get filtered out. Laypeople form their first judgment from the same explanation, so confident, plausible-sounding reasoning can pull them toward the wrong answer. The same tool becomes an asset for one group and a liability for the other.

The experiment compared four approaches: giving only a prediction and confidence score with no explanation, showing similar images alongside, marking important regions with a heatmap, and having an LLM spell out its reasoning in words. Laypeople judged whether a mole was cancerous, while clinicians handled harder differential diagnoses. All four approaches raised laypeople's accuracy, mainly by helping them rule out benign moles. A model fitted with fairness constraints to reduce bias against darker skin tones substantially improved accuracy and narrowed the diagnostic gap across skin tones.

Users most compliant with AI performed worst when working without it. The more explanations were shown upfront, the greater that compliance became. AI outperformed humans when symptoms were subtle, but humans did far better on images with atypical or irrelevant features. The researchers believe it would be better to have users propose their own diagnostic hypothesis first, then add the AI's suggestion to surface other possibilities, rather than making LLM explanations longer. The study was published in Nature Medicine.

OlmoEarth is a family of Earth-observation foundation models from Ai2, pretrained on roughly 10 terabytes of multimodal satellite data. Governments, NGOs, and other organizations are already using it for deforestation monitoring, food security, and wildfire-risk prediction.

If your engineering team is solid, the released models alone are enough. The problem is that most environmental organizations best positioned to use these models lack the infrastructure to cover the full cycle, from data labeling through fine-tuning to large-scale inference. That's why Ai2, which has run Skylight and EarthRanger for more than a decade, built the OlmoEarth platform—infrastructure that connects fine-tuning and evaluation all the way to large-scale inference.

blocks.cap: An example of continent-scale output — a wildfire-risk map covering all of North America

blocks.x: Today the platform finishes inference over continent-scale areas in roughly a day. It processes tens of terabytes of imagery while costs run at a fraction of a cent per square kilometer.

Satellite inference operates at a different scale than ordinary machine learning. Fine-tuning a single foundation model alone moves terabytes of data and takes hours.
