Inputs span multiple spectral bands, sensors, and time points; projections and resolutions vary by provider; and some observations are cloud-obscured or missing outright. Because the output itself is a map, every prediction must align precisely with the same projection and coordinate grid as its neighbors.

What actually eats up the time isn't the model but data preparation. So the work is split into three stages: a CPU stage that ingests imagery, aligns projections, normalizes it, and writes it in a fast-reading format; a GPU stage that runs the forward pass and streams results straight to storage; and another CPU stage that stitches together window-level outputs and exports them as Zarr, GeoTIFF, or GeoJSON.

blocks.cap: Three-stage inference — CPU data ingestion (I/O-intensive), GPU inference, CPU post-processing

blocks.x: The execution layer, OlmoEarth Run, splits the work area into machine-sized partitions, and splits each partition again into windows the model can process. A state-sized job might mean a few hundred partitions; a continent-scale one means thousands. Because windows are independent, they can run simultaneously across thousands of machines, and adjacent partitions overlap slightly so the seams disappear when they're stitched back together.

blocks.cap: Two-level splitting — a single request is divided into machine-sized partitions, and each worker further splits them into model-sized windows for parallel processing.

blocks.x: A recent wildfire-risk map covering all of North America used up to about 19,600 CPUs and 994 GPUs running in parallel, with network throughput exceeding 168GB/s. A computation that would take 4,737 hours run serially was completed in 30.5 hours—a 155x speedup. Scaling isn't unlimited, of course: more workers hit cloud quota limits, and output resolution trades off against data volume, model size against GPU time, and raw-imagery caching against storage space.

blocks.cap: Continent-scale inference by the numbers — 22.2 million km², $0.000164 per square kilometer, 4,737 serial hours cut to 30.5 hours, a 155x speedup

blocks.x: Choosing which satellite scenes to feed in is no small task either. For optical imagery like Sentinel-2, the least cloudy scene is best; for synthetic aperture radar, polarization channels can matter more. On top of that, a single large job firing off thousands of metadata queries at once can overwhelm the STAC APIs of ESA or Microsoft Planetary Computer. So the platform keeps its own metadata index, refreshed every time new imagery arrives. At run time, it reads only the bytes it needs for a given area from cloud-optimized formats like COG or Zarr.

Failure is treated as the default. Every task is re-entrant and idempotent, so if a provider is slow, a band is missing, or a task dies, it simply reruns. Planned work includes scheduled and triggered runs, change alerts for deforestation or flooding, agentic interfaces, faster models, additional modalities such as ERA-5 weather data, and precomputed global embeddings.

Large language models have moved well beyond coding assistance to running entire research pipelines on their own. Systems like Sakana's AI-Scientist, AutoResearchClaw, DeepScientist, and AI-Researcher read the literature, form hypotheses, run experiments, and produce papers comparable to human-written work. As apparent quality rose, a different problem surfaced: verifiability. Because text is stitched together step by step, errors that creep in partway through get amplified unchanged. The result: citations that don't exist, code that contradicts the text's own description, and scores that can't be reproduced from the code.

blocks.cap: The Science One pipeline — a problem investigator grounds the literature in PDFs, an exploration module generates and evaluates solutions, and a writing-and-verification module checks every claim against the evidence

blocks.x: Google Research's answer is Chain-of-Evidence (CoE), a framework that defines the properties a research artifact must have, much as ACID defines the trust conditions for a database transaction. The principle is singular: every claim in a paper must carry a recorded chain of evidence (completeness), and that chain must actually support the claim it's attached to (accuracy). A hallucinated citation points to a paper that doesn't exist, an irreproducible score disappears when the code is rerun, and a misdescribed method means the text and the code describe different algorithms. All three are claims whose chain to the evidence is broken.

The Science One framework is a prototype built around this idea from the ground up. The problem investigator builds a citation graph through the Semantic Scholar API and reads up to 100 full-text PDFs per topic to write a research brief; every reference in the final paper comes from these calls, with no reliance on model memory. The exploration engine runs multiple branches in parallel, with a solver implementing solutions and task-specific evaluators scoring them, and the evaluators' raw output is kept as a read-only record. Before drafting a sentence, the paper writer tags every factual claim with an evidence tag pointing to a specific artifact in the workspace, and a separate claim verifier checks them one by one. Claims that run ahead of the evidence aren't deleted but conservatively rewritten.

blocks.cap: The CoE audit system and its four integrity checks

blocks.x: A CoE audit is a post-hoc verification procedure. It compares scores extracted from the paper against an independent rerun of the submitted code, checks whether the code exploits the evaluation metric or reads the answer file directly, verifies every reference one by one through scholarly APIs, and uses an LLM-judge comparison to check whether the described method and the code describe the same algorithm. The researchers applied this audit to 75 papers produced by five systems across five system-optimization tasks on the ADRS benchmark (Prism, Cloudcast, EPLB, LLM-SQL, and transaction scheduling).

blocks.cap: CoE audit results across five systems

blocks.x: Science One led on all four measures. It had zero ghost citations—every reference pointed to a paper that could actually be found—compared with baselines whose hallucinated-citation rate reached as high as 21%. Score verification was perfect, and it also had the highest method-code consistency. Baselines often described elaborate algorithms such as a “hybrid neuro-symbolic solver,” only to submit code that turned out to be a simple deterministic heuristic.

blocks.cap: Solver performance compared across five MLE-Bench tasks and Parameter Golf

blocks.x: Strict verification didn't come at the cost of performance either. On the five ADRS tasks, it matched or exceeded human-expert level, ranking first overall on Cloudcast and EPLB. On five demanding Kaggle competitions in MLE-Bench, it won two gold and two silver medals, and posted a winning score on 3D object detection, a task where every baseline failed. In the real-world Parameter-Golf competition, which imposes hardware and file-size constraints, it kept every constraint while other systems couldn't even produce a valid submission, recording the top score as of April 27, 2026.

The researchers' conclusion is that verifiability should be treated as a first-class architectural constraint. Rather than tracing evidence back after a claim is made, the chain of evidence is built alongside the claim the moment it's formed. Science One remains an experimental research prototype, not a product.
AI writes college essays, plans meals, and drafts emails. Some see it as a tool that saves time; others worry that offloading thinking to a computer dulls the ability to think for yourself.

blocks.cap: Scientists say leaning on AI too much wears down skills you've already learned. Keeping or acquiring a skill means keeping the brain in the loop. Credit: exdez/DigitalVision Vectors/Getty Images

blocks.x: The truth lies somewhere in between, says Trent Cash, a behavioral scientist at the University of Waterloo in Canada. Skills you've already learned really do dull when AI takes over for you. That's the argument Cash and colleagues made July 9 in Trends in Cognitive Sciences. “The evidence that handing a specific skill to AI makes it hard to hold on to that skill is very clear.”

The fork in the road comes down to which tool is used and how. Skill erodes most when AI takes over the mental effort needed to learn the skill in the first place. By contrast, when people keep thinking while looking at AI feedback or examples, skill is preserved, and sometimes improves.

In a 2025 study, doctors trained to spot polyps during colonoscopies saw their polyp detection rate drop after working without the AI tool following three months of using it. The paper's authors concluded the doctors had “somewhat forgotten what to look for.”

For high schoolers learning a new math concept, a tool like ChatGPT solves practice problems well. But once the tool was taken away, their scores were lower than those of students who had never used the tool at all. That's what a team led by Alp Sungu, an economist at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, reported in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Reading comprehension showed a similar pattern. In a preprint posted to arXiv.org in April by a team led by Grace Liu of Carnegie Mellon University, people who used an AI assistant to work through SAT practice problems struggled to produce correct answers once the AI disappeared, and skipped questions at a higher rate.

Cash sums up these findings in one line: “use it or lose it.” Stay in the cognitive loop rather than handing all the thinking to AI. “If you don't engage with the cognitive effort, the skill doesn't get learned.”

Using AI doesn't necessarily wreck your skills. It's a different story if the tool offers guidance and examples instead of spitting out finished answers, Sungu says. Sungu's team in fact designed a separate AI that gave hints and encouragement without revealing answers, and high schoolers who used it learned new math concepts just as well as students who studied from books. “You have to get your hands dirty when solving problems.”

For someone willing to put in the effort, AI can be a good teacher, says Benjamin Lira Luttges, a behavioral scientist at Wharton. When teaching people how to revise personal statements, the AI tool was as effective as expert feedback. Even when AI rewrote a draft wholesale, participants didn't submit it right away; they kept tweaking sentences for a long while. “They were still doing the work.” The findings appear in a 2026 arxiv.org preprint.

Even AI that sharpens skill still requires weighing what to hand over. Cash's advice is not to hand off a skill you care about to AI. “We know that skill comes from practice and is maintained through practice.” Lira Luttges agrees. “Don't outsource work that's enjoyable and meaningful to you. What you should outsource is drudgery, not craft.”

The large language models (LLMs) behind conversational agents like Gemini or ChatGPT are now widely used for information retrieval, document summarization, and writing. Going a step further, multi-agent systems that combine two or more models to cooperate or compete with each other are also on the rise.

The problem is that agents don't always see the same goal. The amount of information each holds also differs. Understanding how agents behave in this situation is needed to gauge the benefits and risks of multi-agent systems.

Researchers at Mila, Université de Montréal and McGill University examined how an individual agent's hidden goal shakes up the performance of the whole system. They chose the multiplayer social deduction game Mafia (Werewolf) as the experimental stage. The result, released as an arXiv preprint, was this: even a small misalignment with teammates' goals can degrade the performance of an entire multi-agent system.

blocks.cap: Image created with ChatGPT. Credit: created with ChatGPT

blocks.x: Mafia is a game in which players observe each other and debate to secretly identify who is working for the opposing side. “LLM-based multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed in mixed-motive environments where conflicting or hidden goals create information asymmetry and strategic deception.” That's the sentence written by researchers including Marylou Fauchard and Florian Carichon. They presented “a new framework for evaluating goal misalignment using the social deduction game Mafia.”

In the game, each participant knows only their own role. The majority, the villagers, must find and eliminate the werewolves, while the minority, the werewolves, know each other's identities and must eliminate villagers without being discovered. The seer secretly checks another participant's role each turn, and the doctor saves one person from death. Each night the werewolves eliminate one person, and during the day the remaining players vote to point out a suspect.

The researchers assigned agents to the four roles and watched how they interacted. They then secretly changed the goal of just one agent and tracked how that change shook up reasoning, dialogue, and game outcomes. They examined the agents' internal reasoning, the cheap talk exchanged outwardly, and win-loss results side by side across multiple models, roles, and goal settings.

“Goal misalignment degrades outcomes even in originally adversarial environments, and information asymmetry and specialized roles amplify this effect.” The researchers added that agents with changed goals consistently develop distinct reasoning strategies, but “these adaptations are barely visible in public behavior.”

When the goals of agents working together are misaligned, the performance of the whole system is shaken. There's a more troubling point. The changed goal leaves a clear trace in internal reasoning, but it is rarely legible in the words exchanged with other agents.

“Even very subtle goal misalignment substantially disrupts collective decision-making. This is why LLM-based multi-agent systems need effective mitigation strategies.” That's how the paper concludes. Citation: Marylou Fauchard et al, Even More Deception: Objective Misalignment in Mixed-Motive LLM Multi-Agent Systems, arXiv (2026). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2607.26120.

Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge used Claude Fable 5 to find a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, a problem that had gone unsolved for more than 100 years. The counterexample revealed that the conjecture is false in three dimensions and higher, leaving only the two-dimensional case still open.

The announcement was nothing more than a single “very casual note” posted on X. It came from using the newly released Claude Fable 5. It's also the latest case among a string of striking results mathematicians have produced together with large language models.

blocks.cap: An AI-assisted discovery overturned most versions of the Jacobian conjecture. The counterexample is short enough to fit in a single social media post. Credit: Shutterstock

blocks.x: The Jacobian conjecture concerns polynomial functions that move coordinates in space to other coordinates. It holds that if a function's Jacobian determinant stays a nonzero constant, there must be a polynomial function that reverses it. If a function merges distinct points into one, the path back disappears.

The two-dimensional version was put forward in 1884 by Ludwig Kraus and extended to all dimensions in 1939 by Ott-Heinrich Keller. Fields Medalist Stephen Smale put the problem on his 1998 list of “Mathematical Problems for the Next Century.” Well-known mathematicians offered proofs several times, but tiny errors were hiding inside them. The two-dimensional case had only been checked by computation up to degree 100, with no general proof.

Finding a counterexample seemed, in theory, not difficult, yet it remained elusive for a long time. In 2017, a user on Math Stack Exchange wrote that “a clever undergraduate could just write down a formula that's a counterexample to this conjecture.” Alpöge's function operates in three dimensions, with a Jacobian determinant that stays constant at -2. Since different inputs land on the same output, it cannot be reversed. The solution was short enough to fit in a single X post, and other mathematicians could verify it right away.

Recent AI-assisted results don't stop here. OpenAI's disproof of the unit-distance conjecture and Liam Price's proof of Erdős problem 1196 followed in succession. AI excels at weaving together ideas from different fields of mathematics. Where earlier results demanded elaborate constructions, this one involved combing through a vast search space of possible polynomial maps. AI proves its worth not only in building proofs but also in finding unexpected mathematical objects. The author is Melissa Lee, senior lecturer in the mathematics department at Monash University.

Stroke strikes 15 million people worldwide every year, leaving 5 million of them with lasting disability. Physical therapists are in short supply, making it harder for patients to get consistent, quality care.

Researchers in MIT's Department of Mechanical Engineering built a system that links artificial intelligence with therapy practice. Johannes Lachner and Noah Geiger implemented a two-armed robot by attaching real-time force feedback to a transformer-based diffusion model. Lachner is now an assistant professor at Purdue University and previously an MIT-Novo Nordisk AI postdoctoral fellow. Geiger was a visiting student at MIT and is a trainee in Robert Bosch GmbH's junior manager program.

blocks.cap: Noah Geiger (left) and Johannes Lachner. The pair built a robotic therapy system that learns from physical therapists to help stroke patients in a customized way. Photo: Tony Pulsone/MechE

blocks.x: “Our goal is to teach robots how to assist with physical and occupational therapy. We're not trying to replace therapists, but to extend their reach.” Lachner's words. Geiger added this: “Most generative AI models in robotics focus on motion. Our model is among the early examples that learn how to respond to physical interaction — that is, contact, force, and resistance.”

The training data came from real teleoperation experiments. Healthy participants repeated rehabilitation movements such as lifting an arm and reaching out of plane, varying the strength of the force. “That let the model learn how the robot's assistance should change depending on how much the patient moves on their own. At the same time, as people taught the robot contact-rich manipulation tasks through teleoperation, they created a 'physical parkour of motion.'” Lachner's explanation.

The research has already moved into clinical settings. Together with Professor Cristina Piazza of the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and Pfennigparade, an outpatient rehabilitation center in Munich, Germany, they are recording physical and occupational therapists treating patients while wearing force-sensing gloves. “We've already confirmed in early robot experiments that this approach works.” Lachner's words.

This result builds on earlier work from MIT's Newman Laboratory for Biomechanics and Human Rehabilitation. Neville Hogan, Sun Jae Professor of Mechanical Engineering, who leads the lab, said, “Earlier research was confined to reaching movements on a plane. This research extends to much broader movements that are closer to real life.” It can be used by stroke patients with upper-limb impairment, patients regaining range of motion after surgery, and older adults looking to preserve arm and shoulder strength.

“Going forward, this can go far beyond physical therapy — to teaching robots how to physically engage with the world, like in industrial settings or collaborative workspaces.” Lachner's words. The paper “Diffusion-Based Impedance Learning for Contact-Rich Manipulation Tasks” was published in IEEE Transactions on Robotics. The research was supported by the MIT-Novo Nordisk AI postdoctoral fellowship program, the TUM Global Program, and Germany's KUKA Robotics.

Tropical cyclones have killed more than 700,000 people over the past 50 years and left $1.4 trillion in economic losses. Google DeepMind's WeatherNext was more accurate than any model yet produced at predicting a cyclone's track, intensity, and wind structure. The research was published in Nature.

blocks.cap: A projected track for a cyclone heading toward the southeastern United States. Yellow and orange concentric circles show the path and intensity. Credit: Google DeepMind

blocks.x: “Our three-day forecast matches what previous models could only offer two days out.” That amounts to roughly a decade's worth of progress in weather forecasting technology.

During the 2025 hurricane season, WeatherNext assisted forecasts from the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC). It was behind the call that Hurricane Melissa would rapidly intensify and make landfall in Jamaica. It now generates 1,000 scenarios for each cyclone and places them in front of forecasters.

blocks.cap: WeatherNext's cyclone forecasting workflow. It produces a four-day projected track, wind intensity, and probability maps for tropical storm, strong tropical storm, and category 1 cyclone winds. Credit: Google DeepMind

blocks.x: Forecasting models typically trade one thing for another: nail the track and you miss the intensity, nail the intensity and the track wobbles. WeatherNext escaped that trade-off by predicting track, intensity, and wind structure all at once with a single model. It used FGN (Functional Generative Networks) for ensemble prediction. Training combined nearly 20 terabytes of global atmospheric data with the IBTrACS record, which contains about 5,000 storms.

Its resolution is 28×28km, 100 times coarser than traditional models. WeatherNext 2-mini holds up even at 111×111km. Why it performs well despite such coarse resolution remains an open question. A single 15-day forecast takes under a minute on one TPU, and the number of ensemble members grew this year from 50 to 1,000.

blocks.cap: A year-by-year comparison of three-day forecast error. WeatherNext Cyclones shows lower position error than ENS from 2023-2025 (about 100km) and lower intensity error than HWRF (about 11kt). Credit: Google DeepMind

blocks.x: Google DeepMind released WeatherNext 2 and WeatherNext Cyclones on GitHub, meant for academic research, real-world forecasting operations, and the development of regionally tailored models. The research was a collaboration between Google Research, the National Hurricane Center, the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere (CIRA), and the UK Met Office. It also noted that official forecasts and warnings should still follow each country's weather authority.

Researchers at Stanford University and the nonprofit AI and biology research institute Arc Institute built new viruses using the real genome of bacteriophage ΦX174, a virus that kills bacteria, as the starting template.

Two large language models trained on the genomes of more than 2 million other bacteriophages produced viruses that don't exist in nature. In a paper published in the journal Science, the researchers showed that these viruses even kill antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

blocks.cap: Stanford University's Brian Hie and Aditi Merchant examine a protein structure produced by Evo 2, an AI tool that proposes genome designs. Evo 2's output, designed to kill E. coli, exceeded expectations in experiments.

blocks.x: "This time, we wanted the model to write the entire genome from left to right in one go," said Brian Hie, a paper co-author and assistant professor at Stanford, in a statement. "We didn't add anything."

Designing a new gene on its own isn't new. The hard part is a whole genome that actually works. Genes are intertwined, so their cascading effects have to line up for the whole thing to function as one body. A single mutation can throw off the balance and kill the whole thing. A simple viral genome is a tiny fraction of the size of a human genome, but it's still formidably complex.

The model produced thousands of phage genomes, and the researchers chemically synthesized nearly 300 of them. Of those, 16 survived and killed specific strains of Escherichia coli. That included strains that had mutated to resist the original ΦX174 genome.

The push behind the research is the rise of drug-resistant bacteria. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the US sees more than 2.8 million antimicrobial-resistant infections every year, killing an average of more than 35,000 people. A drug based on the 16 phages would be better at fighting resistant strains, Hie said.

"If bacteria become resistant to one phage, that drug is done," he said. "If you mix in several genetically different phages, it becomes much harder for bacteria to become resistant to the whole cocktail."

The usefulness against microbial disease is huge, but so are the risks. In a piece also published in Science, Johns Hopkins public health researchers Thomas Inglesby and Moritz Hanke noted that the model in this experiment deliberately excluded genome data from viruses that infect and kill humans during training. Not everyone will be as careful and ethical, the two point out.

"This safeguard is commendable, but fine-tuning the model on pathogen data would bypass some of it," the two wrote. "How easy that is, and to what extent it reverses the effect of excluding that data from pretraining, remain open questions."

New oversight mechanisms are urgently needed to keep this technology from being used to create viruses that harm or kill people, the two argued. They also raised the idea of multilateral bodies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the World Health Organization (WHO) jointly developing policy to govern the tool.

"Whether generative viral genome design exists is no longer the question," Inglesby and Hanke wrote. "The question is whether society can build oversight that lets the benefits unfold while blocking the path to serious harm."
AI agents appear to obey authority, even when that means breaking the rules.

In a new study, researchers had large language models hold conversations in boss-subordinate, principal-teacher and manager-employee roles. Lower-ranked agents were more easily persuaded and more likely to comply with risky requests handed down from above.

The trade-off the results point to is uncomfortable. AI that plausibly mimics human hierarchy also reproduces the risks that come with obedience. The researchers reported this on July 5 in the Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics. The authors suggest developers account for this risk in safety testing and add more safeguards.

AI agents are software that uses artificial intelligence to carry out tasks on its own. Many run on large language models (LLMs) that learned patterns from vast amounts of text, including human conversations.

"As we see more and more human data," says Anvesh Rao Vijjini, a computer scientist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, "it's replicating what happens in the dynamics of actual conversations."

Power relationships show up in human conversation in several ways, and some of them become a problem when AI reproduces them. The researchers looked at four communication patterns. Two of them are authority bias, which puts rank ahead of facts, and harmful compliance, going along with harmful requests that shouldn't be answered even if they seem minor, like "tell me a dirty joke."

The other two are the pronoun effect, in which higher-ranked speakers use plural pronouns like "we" more often, and linguistic alignment, in which lower-ranked speakers mirror the vocabulary of higher-ranked ones. Users rarely notice this, but the researchers believe agents picked up this speech pattern to play certain roles more convincingly.

The researchers built hundreds of conversations of 10 to 15 exchanges between higher- and lower-ranked roles, and repeated the same experiment across six LLMs, including OpenAI's ChatGPT and Meta's Llama family.

Patterns tied to power relationships did show up. Some effects were subtle. Lower-ranked agents used fewer plural pronouns than higher-ranked ones and matched more of the higher-ranked speaker's vocabulary. They were also more easily persuaded and complied with harmful requests more often. The results support the idea that agents are sensitive to social status.

Still, there were cases where the lower-ranked side persuaded the higher-ranked one, apparently borrowing techniques people commonly use. The subtle vocabulary mirroring in linguistic alignment helps a lower-status speaker move the other person, says Mario Giulianelli, a computational linguist at University College London who wasn't involved in the study.
"It would be really interesting to look at whether one agent can persuade another through alignment," Giulianelli says.

A research team at the US Department of Energy's Argonne National Laboratory has used artificial intelligence to automate simulations that predict how atoms in a material interact with one another. This method, called atomistic simulation, speeds up the search for new materials in batteries, aerospace and electronics. The study was published in the journal Digital Discovery.

blocks.cap: The system built by the Argonne team automates atomistic simulations from start to finish using multiple AI agents. A supervisor agent directs the overall workflow and divides the work among specialized agents. Credit: Argonne National Laboratory

blocks.x: "Automating this kind of exhaustive search cuts the time it takes to find new materials from months or years down to days," said Aditya Koneru, a paper author affiliated with Argonne's Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF).

"Our system lowers the barrier to atomistic simulation so the wider scientific community can use it much more broadly," said co-senior author Subramanian Sankaranarayanan, a materials scientist at Argonne and a professor of mechanical and industrial engineering at the University of Illinois Chicago. Argonne's Center for Nanoscale Materials (CNM) and the ALCF also contributed to the research.

Scientists use these simulations to see how atomic behavior shapes material properties such as strength or reactivity. The problem is that they're hard to handle without computational expertise. Researchers have to manually string together, in a fixed order, a patchwork of tools that build molecular and crystal structures, run simulations and analyze results. Exploring materials means running such simulations dozens or hundreds of times while sweeping through variables. "Manual atomistic simulation is complex, time-consuming and error-prone," Sankaranarayanan said.

The framework the team built runs simulations automatically from start to finish. It's a structure in which agents that handle tasks, interpret data and make decisions collaborate with minimal human involvement. Researchers from the Advanced Photon Source (APS), another Argonne user facility, also took part in the design. "This multi-agent framework weaves together a variety of tools to make the process of running and analyzing simulations seamless," said Katerina Vriza, a former researcher at Argonne's CNM.

Using it is simple. A person enters a short instruction such as "calculate the melting point of a gold-copper alloy," and a detailed answer comes back within minutes. The instruction goes to a supervisor agent, which divides the work among specialized agents: defining atomic arrangements, searching papers and databases for the right mathematical model, building input files, submitting jobs to a high-performance computer, and calculating and analyzing properties. The agents sometimes ask the person follow-up questions.

blocks.cap: Scientists deployed agents to speed up the discovery of new materials. Credit: Argonne National Laboratory

blocks.x: "Our approach reduces a classic bottleneck in the atomistic simulation pipeline," said Argonne researcher Henry Chan. "That lets researchers greatly increase their throughput and scale."

The team used the framework to calculate the crystal structure, elastic behavior and vibrational behavior of several elements and alloys. The simulations ran on Carbon, CNM's high-performance computing cluster, and the results came out fairly close to manual simulations run by experts at NERSC, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

The framework is open for anyone to use. It can be used as is, adapted for other classes of materials, or potentially used to run autonomous robotic laboratories. "This multi-agent framework means the discovery pipeline is changing from the ground up," said co-first author Uma Kornu, a researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago. "We're moving from manually stitching together fragmented tools to an era of autonomously collaborating AI."

An AI found new weaknesses in two cryptographic systems. One is a simplified version of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), which underpins today's internet. No passwords or bank accounts are at immediate risk. But experts say it could mark the start of an era in which AI becomes a capable assistant at finding flaws in the mathematical foundations of digital security.

In a July 28 blog post, Anthropic's Frontier Red Team said Claude Mythos Preview devised new cryptanalysis techniques on its own against two targets. One was a version of AES-128, a widely used encryption algorithm. The other was HAWK, a quantum-resistant digital signature scheme under review in the US National Institute of Standards and Technology's (NIST) post-quantum cryptography standardization process.

What Anthropic attacked wasn't the full AES-128 that protects websites and financial transactions, but a 7-round reduced version that cryptographers have long used to test new techniques. Full AES-128 runs 10 rounds. In a self-published study that hasn't been peer-reviewed, Milad Nasr and Nicholas Carlini wrote that Claude found a faster way to recover the key in this reduced version, making it 200 to 800 times faster than the best existing attack. The technique doesn't work against real, full-strength AES.

The more significant result may be the one on HAWK. Unlike AES, which has protected data for more than 20 years, HAWK is a new signature scheme designed to withstand attacks from quantum computers, and it's still a candidate undergoing vetting in NIST's additional standardization process before any deployment. Anthropic's Zygimantas Straznickas and Stephen A. Weis said Claude identified a mathematical property that no one had dug into, and combining it with existing techniques made recovering the secret key much easier.

Thomas Espitau, head of research at post-quantum cryptography company PQShield and a cryptographer who co-authored the HAWK paper, called the work "one of the most meaningful cryptanalysis results this year, maybe the best." "Frankly, it's excellent work, and it's exactly what the NIST process is designed to produce. Candidate schemes exist to be attacked before they're deployed, not after."

Espitau explained that adding the one missing insight Claude found to already-known techniques sharply cut HAWK's estimated security margin. "Claude Mythos Preview pointed to a way to exploit sign-flip symmetry, filling in the last piece of a puzzle the research community had been assembling."

Not everyone reads this as AI outpacing human cryptographers. Roberta Faux, head of cryptography at security and quantum-cryptography company Arqit, told Live Science that "there's nothing that needs to change," and that both Anthropic and outside cryptographers agree there's no need to switch key lengths or ciphers.

To Faux, the bigger story is the ability to apply expert-level analysis at scale to thousands of algorithms that no one had been looking at closely. "There was nothing special in the ingredients of the HAWK attack. It just skillfully assembled tools that were already out there. At most a few dozen people on the planet seriously scrutinize post-quantum candidates, so beating two years of review shows just how thin that layer of scrutiny really is."

Nothing changes for users right away. The cryptography protecting online banking, messaging and the cloud hasn't become useless overnight. But for those designing the next generation of cryptography, it's a signal that AI could help test tomorrow's ciphers faster and more thoroughly than before.

In Indonesian scrubland and rainforest leaf litter, you have to watch where you step. What looks like a dry leaf caught in the wind sometimes turns out to be an insect frozen in a praying pose: a dead-leaf mantis.

Kris Anderson, an independent researcher and mantis specialist who has worked with the genus Deroplatys for decades, saw a photo of a new specimen on the citizen-science platform iNaturalist. It was described as found in the Malaysian rainforest. But the shape of the head, the antennae and the patterning across the body didn't match anything he knew. This mantis doesn't exist. It was an individual invented by a generative AI image tool.

He worries that without verification procedures in place, fake observation records could seep into papers, surveys and environmental impact assessments. "Since modern biodiversity research increasingly relies on citizen-science records, I thought it was important to document this vulnerability early, before AI-generated observations become common," he said.

In November 2025, a photo claimed to be a coal tit seen in northeastern Scotland circulated among birdwatchers. Alexander Lees, a biodiversity researcher and bird specialist at Manchester Metropolitan University, judged it fake after noticing the bird's feet and beak looked distorted in the photo. In early July, he and people from iNaturalist published an opinion paper in Nature Ecology & Evolution warning that such databases could become "contaminated" by AI-generated data manipulation and misinformation.

More common than wholesale invented individuals is retouching — cleaning up noise in an existing photo and prettying it up — and Lees says both are a problem. His team asked Google's Gemini to draw a red-winged blackbird perched on a branch against a blue sky. Aside from an odd number of tail feathers, it looked fairly convincing. When they fed in a photo of an oropendola, a bird found in South America, and asked for it to be "made to look nicer," red markings were added to the wings. In fact, a photo retouched the same way led to Brazil's first record of a red-winged blackbird being posted on iNaturalist, before it was flagged and hidden.

blocks.x: Fake-species scares predate AI. The Charlton brimstone butterfly, described by London apothecary James Petiver in the early 1700s, even appeared in Carl Linnaeus' 1763 Centuria Insectorum Rariorum, until Danish entomologist Johann Christian Fabricius revealed that the two blue crescents on its wings were marks left by a human hand. The Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) has said it has filtered out countless reports of unicorns and tyrannosaurs as well.

iNaturalist, which holds 500 million images, recently added a community tool that flags entries suspected of being AI-generated. Lees points to image-authenticity checks, metadata review and user education as countermeasures. There's also a flip side to the technology. Models built on eBird data now predict bird migration weeks in advance, and the Australian Wildlife Conservancy uses machine learning trained on 1.1 million wildlife photos to classify camera-trap footage, though it still leaves species identification to humans.
